cells.why: No row ran J's four-roll test. The parts are measured on etcd, not on fero: a handover pauses the group 9.7 to 9.8 ms at the median, and etcd drops the writes caught in it, so A-02 adds 'refuse at once, never drop' (E-13). Three copies in about 1 s is a sum of measured parts with no real machine restart, and the other shapes' handovers (a writer epoch, a seal, a lease, an in-sync set, the outside log) were not run at all.
cells.closes: J's four-roll test on the phase-2 build, on real hosts, with A-02's refuse-at-once rule in the handover
cells.why2: A roll is one planned handover per copy, then a restart and a catch-up. E-13 measured etcd's handover pause at 9.7 to 9.8 ms (worst 31 ms) and reasons about 1 s for three copies on this box, with A-02's rule that a write caught in the transfer is refused at once, never dropped. No roll ran on a v5 kernel, and a real machine restart was not timed.

cells.why: Every log-based row can work the number out (the writer's commit offset minus the copy's own log end and fold position), and API.md names `cluster.me.caughtUp`. But no experiment built the report, or the gate that keeps clients and the roll waiting; with the kernel on a worker the fold's position also sits on another thread (K-20).
cells.closes: v4's early-writable case as a regression test on the phase-2 build (the lag report, the client gate, the roll gate)
cells.why2: The number is how far a copy's log and its fold are behind the leader's commit offset (DESIGN-V5 §6.1, need 4). In a row with one writer per group a restarted copy cannot take a write on its own, so v4's fault cannot come back in the same form. No experiment built the report, or the gate that keeps clients and the next roll step away until the gap closes.

The skip-seed-on-join fix is not in the row, and V4 takes no fix (AMENDMENTS 3).

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. Forwarding alone does not give this: v4 forwards from any member too, and still needs TLS and a client that reconnects only through one address (STATUS.md). What is measured: one client on one wss address to one server reaches its first committed write in 13 to 17 ms (E-40), and 10,000 TLS links cost 538 MB in Node, so a terminator stands in front (E-27, A-11). No test put one proxy address in front of several copies with a write forwarded to its leader (G-25).
cells.closes: the client test through one proxy address on the phase-3 build: a TLS terminator, several copies, a write forwarded to its leader, and a client that never dials a member's own address

cells.why: E-38c measured the failure this guards against: a real etcd member cut from its leader stalled its own clients for the whole fault. A-02 adds 'refuse at once with a redirect', and `smart` clients would route around it, but neither was built, and no test moved a client off a shut server behind one public address.
cells.closes: the failover test on the phase-2 build: a member that cannot forward refuses at once, and the client moves in one retry
cells.why2: A-02 adds the rule: a member that cannot forward a write refuses it at once with a redirect, and a handover refuses the writes caught in it; rows with `smart` clients route around the server instead. E-38c and E-13 measured why it is needed (on etcd a cut-off member stalled its clients for the whole fault, and a dropped write cost a 100 ms or 2 s timeout). The rule was not built or modelled.

The pin itself is written with the build.
cells.why2: E-02's pipeline, in TS, Rust and Go, writes every queued record with one writev and one fdatasync on a journal per process: 2.8 million 100 B appends a second on this disk, and 5.5 µs of CPU per append at 50,000 a second in TS. E-12 shows the shared journal needs 8 to 30 times fewer fdatasyncs than a file per group.

cells.why: A log file per group still commits each group's queue with one fdatasync: 1.39 to 2.25 M appends a second in Node at 16 to 256 groups (E-12, mode b), far over PERF-09's 50,000. Its weak point is the tail, 14 to 20 times the journal's p99 from 256 groups, which is PERF-08's, not this requirement's.
cells.why2: A log per partition still batches: E-12's per-group files kept up with 50,000 appends a second per process at 2,000 groups (ceiling 0.59 million in Node), with an fsync shared only inside one group and a p99 of 189 to 460 ms. Kafka itself, flushing every batch, took 86,344 records a second here (E-09c).

cells.why: Judge 1 is right. E-02's followers are log nodes in shape: each appends the writer's batch to its journal, runs one fdatasync per batch and acks, and the batch commits when a quorum is durable: 2.8 million 100 B appends a second in TS. The log-first draft's node keeps a journal (V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW), and even a file per loglet, the form both judges pass ISR on, shares each fsync and reaches 0.59 to 2.25 million appends a second (E-12), against 50,000. The seal and the shared tier's budget belong to other requirements.

In OBJ a commit is a PUT, and many writes share one PUT inside a commit window by design (E-41 assumes 10 ms). No experiment measured appends per PUT: E-28 timed single 1 KB PUTs (1.37 ms p50 on MinIO).
cells.closes: a pin of appends per PUT against a real object store
cells.why2: A commit is one PUT for every write in a commit window, which is group commit by design, with a PUT in place of an fsync. E-28 timed single 1 KB PUTs only (1.37 ms p50 on MinIO); no batched pipeline ran.

cells.why: Judge 1 is right, and it matches PERF-02 to PERF-07, where both judges fail V4 on the same fact. Confirmed step by step: (1) v4's shell runs one write and one fsync per persist call, in order, and its own comment says many appends per fsync is not built (shell/runtime.ts, `persist`); (2) so single-row writes share no fsync; (3) STATUS.md measured about 250 persisted writes a second per member, and 10,000 single-row writes not all on disk in 20 s, against PERF-09's 50,000: 99.5 % under the bar. Group commit would be a change to the row, and V4 takes no fix (AMENDMENTS 3).

cells.why: The row clause holds with room: 315 to 338 B of heap a small row, 510 to 528 B with the kernel on a worker, against 2 KB (E-05). cells.why: Every copy and every relay holds its own client links and serves reads and subscriptions from what it folds. Followers and relays keep every subscribe property with A-06 (E-31, model-checked on ten bounds), and one Node server holds 10,000 idle links and 1,000 active subscribers on under a fifth of a core (E-27). So each added copy adds that room; the autoscaler sim itself was not run.
cells.why2: Every copy takes client links and serves reads and subscriptions from the replicas it holds, or forwards or redirects the rest, so each added copy adds links and fan-out. E-27 measured one Node server holding 10,000 idle links, and 1,000 active subscribers on 9 to 17 % of a core. The autoscaler sim itself was not run; the claim holds from the shape.

cells.why: The design gives it: a group has `copies` voters out of n members, so a copy applies only the groups it holds, and the row's own way of spreading groups (slot moves, cells, lanes, splits, partitions) adds writers and row room. No autoscaler sim and no 8-copy run with partial replication exists: E-16 healed one group of three voters on four members, and E-18 balanced slots in a simulation of load, not of copies.
cells.why2: A group has `copies` voters, not every member, so a copy applies only its own groups' writes and the cap of five has no cause; added copies take groups by placement, and by slot moves or splits where the row has them. E-18 simulated the move policy up to 64 groups (max/mean at most 1.25 on seven of eight loads). No run had 8 copies with partial replication, and there is no autoscaler sim.

cells.why2: A group has `copies` voters, not every member, so a copy applies only its own groups' writes and the cap of five has no cause; added copies take groups by placement, and by slot moves or splits where the row has them. E-18 simulated the move policy up to 64 groups (max/mean at most 1.25 on seven of eight loads). No run had 8 copies with partial replication, and there is no autoscaler sim.

cells.why: The row has it by design: a log-only voter on the platform's tier is the third voter. But V `+wit` and its 'lead only to repair' rule were never modelled (E-16 starts every group at three full voters), no crash test ran, and the shared tier's budget for OPS-14 (A-29) is not built.
cells.why2: The design has it: with two copies the platform's log tier adds a log replica as the third voter (V `+wit`, N `tier`). No experiment modelled the log replica or its 'lead only to repair' rule (G-25), and the shared tier's budget per tenant, which OPS-14 needs, was not built (E-35: a neighbour's p99 rose 1.40 to 1.59 times without it).

cells.why2: Two copies stay writable after either one's crash when the controller shrinks the in-sync set (SPACE §4.2). The controller's own three voters must sit somewhere, which the row does not say, and nothing here ran it.

cells.why: Durability sits in a log tier of three, so two servers can lose either one by design. But the writer change (a seal and a metadata CAS) was never modelled in this study, and the shared tier's budget for OPS-14 (A-29) is not built.
cells.why2: Durability sits on the log tier, so either of two servers can crash. The seal and metadata step that hands the log to the other server was not modelled here, and the shared tier's budget for OPS-14 was not built (E-35).

cells.why: The object store holds every commit, so either copy's crash takes no vote away. But the lease takeover by CAS on the manifest was never modelled, and no crash test ran.
cells.why2: The object store holds every commit, so either of two servers can crash and the other takes the lease by a conditional PUT (1.37 ms p50 on MinIO, E-28). The lease takeover was not modelled, and the store is a shared tier under OPS-14.

cells.why: The mechanism is model-checked: with two servers and crashes, one writer, no stale judgement, and a write can always commit while `#meta` and one server are up (E-16, 9 rules, all needed). With a tier shared between projects it is still open, because the tier's budget for OPS-14 (A-29) is not built; with a log tier per project it is met.
cells.why2: The crash half is model-checked: two servers, the log members as voters, and a writer handover by a committed writer epoch that is safe and live with 9 rules (E-16). The shared tier must also meet OPS-14, and its budget per tenant was not built (E-35). With a log tier per project that clause falls away.

cells.why: Judge 2 is right. BUY as run (E-44) and as shaped for costing (E-41) keeps its log on three NATS servers of the project's own, with the app's two machines beside them as clients: the shape of SRV and PD, which both judges score 'not'. Every JetStream replica is a full copy (three per stream in E-44), so there is no log-only voter and no platform tier that stands in as the third, and a project cannot run on two copies. A crash of an app machine is harmless, but that is as true of SRV; a NATS tier shared by projects would be SLOG's shape, and it was not run, priced or checked against OPS-14.

cells.why: No row ran the host-loss test. Rows with three voters keep a majority, and a wiped replica never returns under its old id (A-01, A-28: model-checked on etcd's spec); rows that lean on a witness, a log tier or the object store for the free copy were never modelled there (V `+wit`, SLOG's seal, OBJ's takeover), and a shared tier's budget for OPS-14 (A-29) is not built. No row states the one-disk free copy's window, which is the upload lag to the object store (E-41 assumes a minute) or, with no store, the whole disk.
cells.closes: the host-loss test on the phase-2 build, and a stated loss window for the one-disk free copy
cells.why2: A free project's one copy has log replicas on the platform's tier beside it, so a lost host loses nothing by design. The log replica and its repair path were never modelled (G-25), and the shared tier's budget for OPS-14 was not built (E-35).

cells.why2: With three voters on three hosts a majority has every acknowledged write on disk, so one lost host loses nothing: E-14c model-checked the lost-disk replacement (0 stuck states of 340,671, no invariant broken) and E-29 lost 0 of 10,020 acknowledged batches in 2,640 power cuts. Not shown: a host-loss test with the object store, and the stated loss window of a one-disk free copy, which E-41 only assumes as one upload a minute.

cells.why: Step 1: in OBJ a commit is a PUT. Step 2: 10 writes a second, 100 ms apart, cannot share a PUT unless the commit window is over 2 s, so about 26.3 million PUTs a month. Step 3: at $0.005 per 1,000 that is $131, and $135.80 in all, against $10: 13.6 times the bar with the subscribers inside, so neither the restated bar (AMENDMENTS 1.3) nor a likely price error flips it.
cells.why2: Q `put`: a commit is one PUT. At 10 writes/s, 100 ms apart, every write is its own commit: 26.3 million PUTs a month, $131 at $0.005 per 1,000, so $135.80 against $10 with the subscribers inside. That is 13.6 times the bar, too wide for a price read from a search summary to flip, and it is the same under AMENDMENTS 1.3's restated bar; fewer PUTs would mean a commit that waits over 2 s.
